headline: Silence of Titan: the most scientifically accurate space film ever made?
standfirst: Five stars for a thriller that “gets every detail right”
brief: Our critic loved this film and praises its accuracy at length. Letters from physics teachers are already arriving, so check the review before it goes to print.

body.t: From its opening shot, Silence of Titan announces that it takes physics seriously.
When an asteroid explodes far from the orbiting station, the crew see the flash and then, realistically, hear the roar a few seconds later, because sound travels through space more slowly than light.

options: Sound travels through space faster than light.
They would hear the roar first and see the flash afterwards, because the sound starts before the light does.
Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium, so no roar can cross the vacuum of space.
feedback: Sound doesn't travel through space at all, at any speed.
The order isn't the problem. Think about what sound needs in order to travel.
err.fix: When an asteroid explodes far from the orbiting station, the crew see the flash but, realistically, hear nothing, because sound needs a medium and cannot travel through the vacuum of space.
keys: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium.
Space is a vacuum, so the sound cannot reach the crew (light can).

body.t: Inside the station, 400 km above the Earth, the crew float freely because they are too far from the planet for its gravity to reach them.

options: Gravity there is still about 90% of its surface value; the crew and station are in free fall together.
The crew float because the air inside the station holds them up.
Gravity would reach them, but only if the station were stationary; an object moving this fast no longer feels it.
feedback: The air provides a negligible buoyancy force compared with an astronaut's weight.
Gravity acts on an object whether or not it is moving.
err.fix: Inside the station, 400 km above the Earth, the crew float freely because they and the station are in free fall together, accelerating towards the Earth at the same rate.
keys: Gravity is still strong at this height.
The crew and the station are in free fall together, so there is no contact force on the crew.

body.t: In one tense scene, an astronaut pushes a heavy crate away from her and drifts backwards in the opposite direction.
body.ok: It is correct: by Newton's third law the crate pushes back on her with an equal and opposite force.

body.t: Later, when the station's engines fail, the crew have only minutes before it falls straight to Earth, since an orbit needs the engines to keep pushing against gravity.

options: Without engines, the station would fly off in a straight line away from the Earth, because nothing would then hold it in.
An orbit needs no thrust: gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the station moving in a circle.
The engines push the station towards the Earth, so if they fail the orbit grows.
feedback: Gravity still acts when the engines stop, so the station would not move in a straight line.
Engines are not needed for a steady orbit, in either direction.
err.fix: Later, when the station's engines fail, the crew are in no immediate danger, since gravity alone provides the centripetal force that keeps the station in orbit.
keys: No thrust is needed to maintain a circular orbit.

body.t: The action then moves to Saturn's moon Titan, which has a thick atmosphere, so the characters can hear sounds around them through their helmets.
body.ok: It is correct: Titan has a dense atmosphere, which is a medium that sound can travel through.

body.t: A nice detail is that the astronauts' weight is far smaller on Titan, even though their mass has not changed.
body.ok: It is correct: mass stays the same, while weight depends on the gravitational field strength, which is much smaller on Titan.

body.t: The sound design is equally clever: as the rover drives away, its warning siren rises in pitch, just as it would in real life.

options: The pitch would not change at all, because the siren's own frequency is constant however the rover moves.
The pitch would rise only if the air were moving with the rover.
For a source moving away, the waves reach the listener stretched out, so the pitch is lower.
feedback: The siren emits a constant frequency, but the observed frequency changes when the source is moving.
The motion of the rover alone is enough to change the observed frequency, and it lowers it.
err.fix: The sound design is equally clever: as the rover drives away, its warning siren sounds lower in pitch than when it is at rest, just as it would in real life.
keys: A source moving away gives a longer observed wavelength.
So the observed frequency, and the pitch, are lower.

body.t: And when the captain radios Earth from 1.4 billion kilometres away, the reply comes back with no delay at all, because radio waves travel instantly.

options: Radio waves travel at the speed of sound, so the delay would be years.
Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so even one way takes about 78 minutes over this distance.
Radio waves travel faster than light through a vacuum, so the delay would be only seconds.
feedback: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, not sound.
Nothing carries a signal faster than light. Try $t = d/c$ with $d = 1.4 \times 10^{12}$ m.
err.fix: And when the captain radios Earth from 1.4 billion kilometres away, each message takes about 78 minutes to arrive, because radio waves travel at the speed of light.
keys: Radio waves are electromagnetic and travel at the speed of light.
